newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Sep inflation up after falling for 3 months.
newsitem.headline: French Sep inflation up after falling for 3 months.

text.p: French consumer prices rose in September after falling for three consecutive months, helping allay fears of deflation.
Prices rose 0.4 percent in September, national statistics institute INSEE said on Friday.
Year-on-year, consumer prices rose 1.6 percent, the same as in August and down from 2.0 percent in September 1995.

The September rise came after a monthly drop of 0.3 percent in August following falls of 0.2 percent in July and 0.1 percent in June, which prompted some politicians to warn of a risk of deflation in the French economy.
But economists said then it was risky to read too much into data skewed by a traditional summer drop in fresh food prices.
Economists said the September figures were more or less in line with expectations and would have no influence on Bank of France policy in setting interest rates.

The Bank of France traditionally tracks Bundesbank rate moves closely, keeping a narrow premium over German rates to cushion the franc against any attack by the currency markets, and is very rarely influenced by monthly inflation data.
It has set a goal of keeping inflation below two percent year-on-year.
"A lower number would have increased pressure on the Bank (to cut rates) but with 1.6 percent the pressure does not rise," Morgan Stanley economist Eric Chaney said.
Economists said the rise did nothing to change their outlook for inflation in France this year.
"We're not going to change our outlook because of this report," David Naude, economist with JP Morgan, said. "We're still expecting inflation to fall to about 1.5 percent this year."
"The rises came from the expected areas," Naude added, "Essentially food products reversed their declines of the last few months as did energy and textiles."
The government has said it expects year-on-year inflation of 1.5 percent this year and next.
